title: Adding AI without turning the product into a chat box
metaTitle: AI product design on the field in use
excerpt: Put an AI assist on the field the person was already editing. A blank chat is a new product they did not open the screen to learn.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The sketches are a product surface already in progress, which is where an assist belongs.
caption: The assist belongs on the screen already being drawn. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should an AI assist sit in a product?
faqs.answer: Put it on the field, draft, or selection the person was already editing. Name the action, such as shorten or draft from the specs, and put the result in that field. A blank chat asks them to learn a new product before they can finish the job they opened.

faqs.question: When is a chat the right interface?
faqs.answer: Use a conversation when the job itself is a question. Even then, offer the few questions people actually ask, grounded in the record on screen. Keep billing, deleting, and emailing on their own controls. A sentence in a transcript should not carry a side effect.

faqs.question: What if the source for a suggestion is empty?
faqs.answer: Say what is missing and leave the field alone. Do not invent a plausible title, price, or date. Check the empty case, the partial case, and a person who edits heavily before you add a second control.

markdown:
AI product design can add an assist without turning the product into a chat box. Put the help on the field, the draft, or the selection the person was already editing. A blank conversation is a new product. It asks them to learn how to prompt before they can finish the job they opened the screen to do.

People came in to write, to sort, to price, to reply, or to configure. Meet them there. The model works behind a control they already understand: rewrite this, suggest a title, fill from the record, explain this error.

## The job is already on the screen

Start from the screen that exists. Find the moment someone stalls. A title field left empty. A reply box with the facts scattered in tickets above it. A form where three fields always come from the same record. A table cell that requires a calculation the person does in their head.

The assist belongs on that stall. A control beside the field, or a suggestion inside it, that uses the material already on the page. The person invokes it when they want it. The result lands in the field. They edit and move on.

A chat box at the corner of the same screen splits attention. Now there are two products: the one they were using, and a conversation about the one they were using. They have to describe the stall in prose, then carry the answer back by hand. You have added a step and called it help.

An example, labeled as an exercise: a catalog tool for a small brand. The product title and the short description are empty. A control labeled "Draft from the specs" reads the material, dimensions, and price already entered, and fills the two fields. The merchant edits the adjective and saves. There is no panel asking them to "ask anything." The specs were the prompt.

## What the control should say

Name the action, not the technology. "Shorten" is a control. "Ask AI" is a lobby. The label should tell the person what will change and what will be left alone. "Shorten to two sentences" is better than "Improve," because improve is a judgment they did not hand over.

Show the source in a line next to the result, and state the limit. This draft uses the specs on this page and does not know about the size that is out of stock. The person needs that sentence in the moment, because the next thing they do is decide whether the draft is fit to keep.

Discard and edit are the real controls. Accepting a suggestion should never be the only comfortable path, and it should never publish, send, or charge by itself. The field is a draft until the person saves the way they always saved.

If the assist cannot run because the source is empty, say what is missing and leave the field alone. Do not invent a plausible title. A blank with a hint is more trustworthy than a fluent guess.

The W3C notes that [WCAG](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) applies to AI web interfaces, under principles that include operable and understandable. A control on a field can meet that bar: it has a name, it can be reached, and the outcome is visible in the field. A chat transcript is harder to operate, harder to scan, and easier to misread as the product's own voice.

## When a conversation is actually the job

Sometimes the job is a conversation. A research tool where the question is the work. A support console where the agent is already in a thread. Even then, structure the thread. Offer the three questions people actually ask, grounded in the record on screen, rather than a single empty input that implies the model knows the company.

Keep the product's navigation, its data, and its actions outside the transcript. The chat can propose. Buttons that bill a customer, delete a row, or email a list stay where they were, with their own confirmations. A sentence in a transcript should not be an action with side effects.

If you feel pressure to add the blank box because competitors have one, check whether your stall is real. A box that nobody can explain in the team's own product is a feature for a demo. It will collect prompts the product cannot answer well, and those answers will define the product more than the screen you designed.

## Keep the product the same idea

The assist should sound and look like the rest of the interface. Same type, same tone, same restraint. A chat panel with a different personality is a second brand inside the tool. Hanabi's product work, on interfaces such as Got Next and Leadly, aims at a focused job rather than a room full of options. An assist that respects that focus sits on the job. It does not open a new room.

Do not add the assist to every field to make the investment visible. One or two stalls, done clearly, teach people that the suggestion is worth a look. A sparkle on every label teaches them to ignore sparkles.

Test the control the way you test any other control. Empty source, partial source, and a person who edits heavily. The empty case should explain what is missing. The partial case should use only what is there and say so. The heavy edit is a sign the draft is a starting point, which is acceptable, or a sign it is noise, which means the control should come off that field. Watch five real sessions before you add a second control.

The trust conditions still apply. Source, limit, and an easy edit are what make the suggestion usable. Without them, a field-level assist is just a smaller place to be confidently wrong. Those conditions are the subject of [designing an AI feature people can trust](/blog/ai-features-people-trust).

If you want the assist designed into the product you already have, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio would rather put help on the field than hand the interface over to a prompt.
